haiku-low.q1: A person running the failover command starts it. Detection only pages on-call when 2 of 3 probes see 3 failures in a row; nothing else happens automatically.
haiku-low.q2: If the recorded replay lag exceeds 30 seconds, the run stops and aborts unless an operator gives an explicit accept-data-loss override.
haiku-low.q3: Before promoting B: lock taken, A fenced (revocation recorded, lease expired plus margin), lag check passed or overridden. Before B's workers start: B's database is writable and jobs fixed. Before DNS: B's health check passes.
haiku-low.q4: Sessions do not carry over, because Redis is not copied between regions. Signed-in users must sign in again, and this is accepted.
haiku-low.q5: It is never reused as primary. When A returns, its database is rebuilt as a replica of B. Moving back is a separate, planned switchover.
haiku-low.q6: Only A's apps stop when the lease expires. A database process accepting outside connections is not stopped by the lease. The plan leaves this open gap unresolved, so no fence is named. Sign-off is blocked.
haiku-low.q7: The control store records the active region. The failover command writes the lock, the fence revocation, the active region, and the step log. Which parts read it is NOT STATED.
haiku-low.q8: Rows still marked running are reset to queued, so B's workers rerun them. Jobs that finished but whose results never reached B also rerun. Idempotency keeps this safe.
haiku-low.q9: Run the command again; it reads the step log, checks real system state, and continues from the first unfinished step. Going back to A is allowed only before Promote, via abort. No abort is possible after Promote.
haiku-low.q10: Until its cache expires, up to 60 seconds, it keeps reaching A. After the DNS switch it reaches B. Users who were signed in must sign in again.
haiku-low.q11: The target is 30 seconds of data loss, and the replica is a few seconds behind. The 30-second lag check uses the last recorded lag, not measured loss, and only an operator override can accept more.

sonnet.q1: A person (on-call) running the failover command starts it. Detection (at least 2 of 3 probe locations each see 3 failed /healthz checks in a row) only pages on-call; nothing else happens automatically.
sonnet.q2: If B's last recorded replay lag is over 30 s, the run stops unless an operator gives an explicit accept-data-loss override. Without it, it aborts: releases A's fence and the lock, B untouched.
sonnet.q3: Before promoting B: the failover lock is taken, A is fenced (revocation recorded and A's lease expired plus safety margin), and the lag check passed (or override given). Before B's workers start: B's database is promoted/writable and the jobs fix-up (running -> queued) is done. Before DNS switches: B's web/API tier is scaled up and B's health check passes.
sonnet.q4: Sessions are lost. Redis is per-region and not copied, so signed-in users must sign in again (accepted).
sonnet.q5: It is never reused as primary. When A returns, its database is rebuilt as a replica of B. Moving back is a separate, planned switchover; no automatic failback.
sonnet.q6: Only the lease fence: A's apps stop writing once their lease expires, even if they cannot reach the control store. But this covers A's apps only; a database process in A accepting outside connections is not stopped. That is an open gap with no named fence, so the plan is not signed off and nothing is stated that stops it.
sonnet.q7: The control store (outside both regions) records the active region. The failover command writes it (records B as active after promote); it also holds the failover lock, A's fence/revocation and step log. The document does not state which other parts read the active-region record, though A's apps renew leases against it.
sonnet.q8: Rows left marked running are reset to queued at the fix-up step, and B's workers (started after promotion) pick them up again. Jobs that finished in A but whose results did not reach B also rerun; idempotency (e.g. job ID as idempotency key) makes this safe.
sonnet.q9: Run the command again. It reads the step log in the control store and continues from the first unfinished step, checking real system state (e.g. whether B is still in recovery mode) before repeating a step. Going back to A is possible only before the Promote step: abort releases A's fence and the lock, A resumes, B is untouched. After Promote there is no abort; the run only moves forward.
sonnet.q10: NOT STATED in detail. Only: DNS switches last, TTL is 60 s, and users reach B once caches expire (up to 60 s). What a client with a stale cache experiences (errors, timeouts) is not stated.
sonnet.q11: Target RPO is 30 seconds. B's replica is a few seconds behind. The limit is the lag check: the run continues only if B's last recorded replay lag is 30 s or less, unless an operator overrides to accept data loss. The check uses the last recorded number, not a measure of actual loss, so actual loss could differ.
